slides.title: Lead Yourself First
slides.body: Before you lead a club, a shift, or a group project, you lead yourself. Choose a standard this week and practice keeping it when someone is counting on you.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Bring one ordinary responsibility
slides.body: Set aside about 50 minutes, then try your plan over seven days. Think of a practice, club meeting, volunteer shift, class project, or first job where your choices affect someone else. A title is optional. The lessons come from Part I of Brenen Morse’s hospitality field guide, The Little Black Book on Leadership.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Part I · You
slides.body: The book moves through five parts: You, Your People, Environment, Techniques of Leadership, and Culture Overhaul. Chapters 1–9 begin with the person making the next choice. By the end you’ll have two or three standards, an ownership rewrite, a seven-day plan, and a skill you can help someone practice.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Restaurant story · The Heritage Honey night
slides.body: In the Preface, Brenen describes running the kitchen the night a Heritage Honey post sent the store sideways. The staff and systems were there. In his account, the missing piece was leadership that could get the team back on course. Think of a group that already knew its material and still needed someone to call the next step.
slides.aria: Restaurant story · The Heritage Honey night
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Conviction shows up in a choice
slides.body: A standard is something another person can watch you do. If you care about accurate work, your standard might be checking the source of a statistic before the group puts it on a slide. Someone watching can see whether you kept that promise.
slides.aria: Conviction shows up in a choice
slides.quote: Leadership does not begin with strategy, systems, or growth. It begins with conviction - with knowing who you are, what you believe, and what you are willing to protect, even when it costs you.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 1: Who You Are
slides.notes: Ask for a visible choice another person could notice.

slides.title: Start with your own work
slides.body: Picture asking a teammate to arrive prepared. What would they find if they looked at your notes or watched you set up? Pick one behavior you could demonstrate before asking someone else to try it.
slides.quote: But before you can lead anyone else well, you must first lead yourself.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 1: Who You Are
slides.notes: Ask for a visible choice another person could notice.

slides.title: Find somewhere you already lead
slides.body: A volunteer who puts the supplies where everyone can find them changes how the next person starts. A project partner who sends an early warning about a missing source gives the group time to adjust.
slides.fieldLabel: Name one place where someone relies on what you do. Finish this sentence with an action: When I ___, it helps the next person ___.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: What is an ethos?
slides.body: Ethos is the set of beliefs that guides your choices under pressure. You might prefer early meetings, value fairness, and live by a rule that you give everyone credit for the work they did. Notice which of those you would protect even in a room full of friends.
slides.chapter: Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.quote: A preference is something you hold when it is convenient. A value is something you say matters. But your ethos is deeper than both.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.notes: Give a work example about keeping a promise. Leave personal beliefs private.

slides.title: Name what a standard might cost you
slides.body: Recording the hours you actually worked might mean a smaller paycheck. Telling the group that your slide is late might cost you a comfortable afternoon. For each choice, you can point to the action and the cost.
slides.aria: Name what a standard might cost you
slides.chapter: Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.quote: If your values have never cost you anything, it is worth asking whether they are truly values at all. Because the real test of what you believe is not what you say in a calm room. It is what you protect when it becomes expensive — when it costs you time, comfort, a relationship, popularity, or even results.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.notes: Give a work example about keeping a promise. Leave personal beliefs private.

slides.title: A center you can return to
slides.body: Brenen names his Christian faith as his own center. For your practice, choose a standard you would protect even if it cost you something. You can keep your personal beliefs private.
slides.aria: A center you can return to
slides.chapter: Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.quote: Your immovable rock may look different than mine. It might be an unyielding code of service, a deep-seated respect for human dignity, or a family legacy you are determined to honor. The operational argument here is not that you must share my specific center; it is that you must have one—named, decided, and unshakable—before the heat of a crisis forces a compromised choice upon you.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.notes: Give a work example about keeping a promise. Leave personal beliefs private.

slides.title: Pick the standards you will keep
slides.body: A broad word like respect becomes easier to keep when you give it a behavior: speak up when a teammate is mocked, even if a friend started the joke.
slides.aria: Pick the standards you will keep
slides.chapter: Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.quote: Every leader talks about values. Very few can tell you what those values have cost them.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 2: The Hills You Die On
slides.fieldLabel: Write three values on paper. Circle two you would protect when it is inconvenient. Beside each, write one action someone could see and what it might cost you. Use those actions for the standards box on your plan.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Find the part you can change
slides.body: Late group slide? Check whether you agreed on a deadline. Missed the start of a shift? Check where you looked for the schedule. Messy close? Check whether you handed off an unfinished task. A useful reply names your part and a repair you can make.
slides.aria: Find the part you can change
slides.quote: When leaders blame their team, they give up their power to change the outcome.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 3: Own the Change
slides.notes: Separate the part the student controls from the repair they can make next.

slides.title: Rewrite a blame sentence
slides.body: In a group project, “They didn’t tell me” leaves you waiting. “I didn’t confirm the deadline. I’ll ask today, then add it to our shared calendar” gives the group a next step. Your part can be small and still be real.
slides.quote: This is not about guilt. It is about power. Owning the change gives you the power to change things. Blame takes that away. When you are tempted to point outward, point inward first.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 3: Own the Change
slides.fieldLabel: Pick a small mix-up. Write the first blame sentence that comes to mind. Under it, write what you controlled, the repair you will make, and when. Leave other people’s private information out.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: The three after-action questions
slides.body: An after-action review is a short look back while you still remember what happened. For a practice, meeting, or shift, put your own choices in every answer. For tomorrow’s change, pick something you can actually do.
slides.quote: What went well? What did not go well? And what will I do differently tomorrow? These questions should all be directed at you, the leader - not the team.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 3: Own the Change
slides.notes: Separate the part the student controls from the repair they can make next.

slides.title: Run a five-minute review
slides.body: Suppose your study group finished the practice problems, then left before deciding who would bring the answers next time. You could keep the part that worked and use the last minute of the next session for a handoff.
slides.fieldLabel: Think of one event from the past week. Take one minute to write what you did that helped, one to identify a miss, and three to choose a change for next time. State it as an action you control.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Practice check · Leading yourself
slides.body: Try all three questions about acting without a title, keeping a standard when it costs something, and owning a mistake. Check your answers and use the explanations to revisit an idea.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: The weight of responsibility
slides.body: A captain can feel rattled after a loss and still give the next player a clear instruction. A shift lead can feel overwhelmed and ask the manager to cover a station. Steadiness can sound like calmly telling someone exactly what help you need.
slides.quote: You do not get to have a bad day in public. Not because your feelings do not matter. But because the team’s stability depends on your steadiness.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 4: The Weight of Responsibility
slides.notes: Let the learner choose a support role without naming anyone.

slides.title: Choose someone you can be honest with
slides.body: Having feelings is part of being human. If a hard day is spilling onto teammates, ask for a pause or support. A trusted adult, mentor, coach, or friend can help you talk it through. If someone is hurting you or you feel unsafe, reach a trusted adult or manager now.
slides.aria: Choose someone you can be honest with
slides.quote: But you also cannot carry the weight alone forever.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 4: The Weight of Responsibility
slides.notes: Let the learner choose a support role without naming anyone.

slides.title: Your expectations shape how you teach
slides.body: First-job example: a new coworker pauses at the register. If you grab the screen every time, they lose the next attempt. Point to the next step, let them try when it is appropriate, and stay nearby for the question.
slides.aria: Your expectations shape how you teach
slides.quote: Every leader carries a belief about people. Most never say it out loud.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 5: What You Believe
slides.notes: Ask what a teacher or helper would do differently at the next attempt.

slides.title: Make belief practical
slides.body: Give a beginner an accurate example, time to practice, and clear feedback. If an entry on a sample order is wrong, name the exact line and ask them to try that part again. The same accuracy standard can stand while someone learns.
slides.quote: This is not naïve optimism. It is disciplined belief.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 5: What You Believe
slides.notes: Ask what a teacher or helper would do differently at the next attempt.

slides.title: Pair one expectation with one kind of help
slides.body: Expecting someone to learn a play is more useful when you also draw the route, walk it with them, and let them try it once.
slides.aria: Pair one expectation with one kind of help
slides.quote: And over time, you will be proven right - because people rarely rise above the level of expectation placed on them.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 5: What You Believe
slides.fieldLabel: Choose a skill in a club, a class project, or a first job. Write one observable expectation and one thing you will do to help someone reach it. Use a role such as new volunteer.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Show up the same way
slides.body: Notice which promise disappears when the week gets busy. If you check the equipment before Monday practice, what will remind you to give Friday’s team the same check? Attach the action to a cue that already happens.
slides.quote: Intensity is easy for leaders. Consistency is difficult.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 6: Consistency Over Intensity
slides.notes: Return to the Friday example. Would a classmate see the same routine?

slides.title: Compare two weeks of effort
slides.body: An all-nighter might finish one assignment. A 25-minute block most afternoons gives you time to notice gaps before the deadline. At practice, teammates can plan around a warm-up that starts on time after a win and after a loss.
slides.quote: Your team does not need a single inspiring speech. They need a leader who shows up the same way every day. They need someone who enforces the same standard on Monday and on Friday.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 6: Consistency Over Intensity
slides.notes: Return to the Friday example. Would a classmate see the same routine?

slides.title: Look back at seven days
slides.body: To check a habit like arriving with the supplies ready, count only the days you actually had the chance. One missed day is information about where the routine broke.
slides.fieldLabel: After marking the grid, write one cue that could help next time.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Give someone else the next turn
slides.body: You can finish a signup sheet fastest by making every change yourself. You can also show a new club member how to add a row, let them add the next one, and check it together. The second choice leaves someone else able to do the work.
slides.aria: Give someone else the next turn
slides.chapter: Chapter 7: Your Job is Their Success
slides.quote: The real job of a leader is to make other people successful. That is the shift.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 7: Your Job is Their Success
slides.notes: Let the learner practice explaining one step and handing the task back.

slides.title: Field story · Catching the ball
slides.body: Brenen uses his Little League story to make a point about helping another person succeed. Think about the player receiving a throw: their part matters to the teammate who threw it. In a group project, the equivalent might be checking that the next presenter can open your file and knows where to start.
slides.chapter: Chapter 7: Your Job is Their Success
slides.notes: Let the learner practice explaining one step and handing the task back.

slides.title: Plan a teaching turn
slides.body: Pick something you could demonstrate in a few minutes. Describe the action, give the learner a turn, and ask them to show you which step they would repeat next time.
slides.chapter: Chapter 7: Your Job is Their Success
slides.quote: Not “How do I get this done?” but “How do I help them become someone who can get this done well?”
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 7: Your Job is Their Success
slides.fieldLabel: Name one skill you will teach this week. Write when you’ll show it, what the other person will do themselves, and one sign they are ready to try again.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Connect the person you want to be to today
slides.body: If you want people to describe you as dependable, choose the action for your next work block. An early update about a delay tells teammates more than an ambition written at the top of a notebook.
slides.aria: Connect the person you want to be to today
slides.chapter: Chapter 8: What You Want to Be
slides.quote: So the question is not just what do you want to be. The question is what are you doing today - right now, this shift - to move closer to that?
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 8: What You Want to Be
slides.notes: Ask for an action small enough to try today.

slides.title: What is it like to work with you?
slides.body: Imagine a volunteer finishing their first hour beside you. What could they honestly say? “I knew where to put the supplies because we walked through it together” gives you a habit to repeat. Write a modest description that you could make true today.
slides.aria: What is it like to work with you?
slides.chapter: Chapter 8: What You Want to Be
slides.notes: Ask for an action small enough to try today.

slides.title: Give the credit and keep the standard
slides.body: Humility might mean admitting you mixed up the assignment. Conviction might mean rechecking the draft before the team submits it, even when a friend wants to skip that step. Both can happen in the same conversation.
slides.aria: Give the credit and keep the standard
slides.quote: The best leaders are not the loudest or the most charismatic. They are often the quietest. What sets them apart is a rare combination: deep personal humility paired with fierce professional conviction.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 9: Humility and Conviction
slides.notes: Name the contribution and who actually made it.

slides.title: Mini case · Credit the quiet researcher
slides.body: A teammate found the sources that carried your presentation. When the group gets thanked, give a specific account: our researcher found the original studies and checked the dates. If a source is still missing, own your part in getting it checked before submission.
slides.aria: Mini case · Credit the quiet researcher
slides.quote: Humility is not weakness. It is the discipline to put the team above your ego. And conviction is not aggression. It is the refusal to lower the standard, even when it would be easier to look the other way.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 9: Humility and Conviction
slides.notes: Name the contribution and who actually made it.

slides.title: Six traps to recognize
slides.body: Waiting for a title leaves an ordinary task undone. A big speech can hide a missed daily habit. Blaming everyone blocks a repair. Owning harm done to you puts responsibility in the wrong place. Making an exception for a friend makes the standard hard to trust. Keeping every worry to yourself makes it harder to ask for help. Pick the trap most likely to affect your next meeting. Bring harassment, discrimination, violence, or a safety issue to a trusted adult, advisor, or manager.
slides.quote: There is a loneliness to leadership that no one warns you about.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 4: The Weight of Responsibility
slides.notes: Let the learner choose a support role without naming anyone.

slides.title: Walkthrough · Review a missed handoff
slides.body: Work through a sample club meeting on paper. Pause to answer the three after-action questions, choose a repeatable cue, and decide how to restart after a missed day. The written script and annotations are ready to use now.
slides.notes: Follow the annotated demonstration and narration script. Pause where the learner is asked to try a step.

slides.title: A resume bullet needs an action you took
slides.body: Suppose you actually ran weekly recaps and changed where everyone found the supply list. “Ran a five-minute recap after club meetings and moved the supply list into our shared agenda” tells a reader what changed. “Visionary leader” leaves them guessing. Use an example only when it matches your own experience.
slides.aria: A resume bullet needs an action you took
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Draft a line you can explain
slides.body: Start with an action you took in a club, class, shift, practice, or volunteer role. Add a result you personally observed. If you are still planning the action, keep a practice note and come back after you’ve tried it.
slides.aria: Draft a line you can explain
slides.fieldLabel: Finish the draft with facts you can explain: I did ___; as a result ___. Omit any unmeasured number. You can decide later whether to include the draft on your resume.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Plan the next seven days
slides.body: Choose one standard, one way you will own a miss, and a five-minute after-action you can repeat. Pick at least three days in the next seven with a real opportunity to practice. Put a cue beside each day, such as when I close my notebook after practice.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: My Standards and First Week Plan
slides.body: Download the sheet and fill it on your own device or on paper. Keep two or three standards, one ownership rewrite, one after-action, a seven-day grid, and one skill you will help someone practice. You may also jot down a trusted person’s role for yourself.
slides.aria: My Standards and First Week Plan
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Optional next step · Leadership Rhythm
slides.body: Leadership Rhythm is a free iPhone and iPad app (App Store, rated 4+) that uses timed intervals to prompt you to notice and recognize people during a shift or practice. Brenen built it to go with Chapter 20 of the book. You do not need it to finish this class. If you use an iPhone or iPad with iOS or iPadOS 16.4 or later and you want a reminder to look up and notice what someone is doing right, you can find it on the App Store.
slides.notes: A clock, a timer or a paper reminder also works. Always offer the no-app path.

slides.title: Part I in one pass
slides.body: Chapters 1–3 ask you to name who you are, decide what you will protect, and own a repair. Chapters 4–6 ask you to seek support, give people room to grow, and keep small promises. Chapters 7–9 bring it back to your team: teach someone, act today like the person you want to become, and give away credit while keeping the standard.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: From the book’s Final Word
slides.body: Think of the next ordinary moment when somebody will count on you. Which part of your plan could they see you carry out then?
slides.quote: The goal is not to become the loudest leader in the room. The goal is to become the steadiest. That is leadership.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Final Word.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Next · See and Develop People
slides.body: Part II takes the next step in Chapters 10–12. You will look for humility, effort, and coachability, ask what someone wants to become, and learn what already motivates them. You can use this week’s teaching turn as a starting point.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Your optional completion record
slides.body: Once you pass the final quiz, you can preview “Lead Yourself First — completed on FirstCareerSteps” or choose a skill you actually practiced. Completion records describe a class you took. They do not award school credit or an accredited certificate. Any addition to your resume needs your confirmation.
slides.notes: The student chooses whether to preview and confirm an addition.

slides.title: Final question 1 · Where leadership begins
slides.body: Think back to how conviction showed up in a choice someone could see.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final question 2 · Own the change
slides.body: Look for the response that gives the leader something they can repair.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final question 3 · The standard on Friday
slides.body: Imagine the same team on a calm morning and on its busiest afternoon.
slides.aria: Final question 3 · The standard on Friday
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final question 4 · Helping someone succeed
slides.body: Recall the chapter about giving another person the next turn at a skill.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final question 5 · An earned resume bullet
slides.body: Assume the learner did the action described and can explain the outcome. Choose the line that gives a reader specific evidence.
slides.aria: Final question 5 · An earned resume bullet
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Review your five answers
slides.body: A score of 4/5 completes the class. Read the reason beside each answer. You can revisit any slide and retake the quiz as often as you need.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Put the first day on your calendar
slides.body: Open your seven-day plan and choose the first real opportunity to use it. If a meeting is canceled, mark no opportunity and pick the next one. After the third practice day, look for one thing you can keep and one thing you would change.
slides.aria: Put the first day on your calendar
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Start with the next promise
slides.body: Carry one line from your plan into the next shift, meeting, practice, or project. Show the standard, let someone else try a skill, and take five minutes afterward to review your own part.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

mid.prompt: A group project has no official leader. Which action applies Chapter 1?
options: Wait until the class votes on a title.
Name the standard you will keep and check your own work against it.
Tell everyone else which values they should have.
mid.why: Conviction shows up in a choice you can make yourself. A student can act on a standard before anyone assigns them a role.

mid.prompt: Which action shows an ethos at work, even when keeping it costs you something?
options: Choose an early meeting because it suits your schedule.
Say honesty matters when everyone already agrees.
Correct an overstated timesheet even though it means a smaller paycheck.
mid.why: A preference can depend on convenience. Giving up a benefit to keep an honest record shows what you will protect under pressure.

mid.prompt: The group misses a slide deadline. Which reply shows ownership?
options: I didn’t check the due time. I’ll confirm it today and update our shared calendar.
They should have reminded me.
Everything anyone else does is my fault.
mid.why: The first reply identifies the part the speaker controlled and a specific repair. Taking responsibility for another person’s harmful conduct is never the assignment.

final.prompt: In Chapter 1, where does leadership begin?
options: With a title or formal plan.
With knowing who you are, what you believe, and what you will protect.
With being the most intense person in the room.
With having the best systems first.
final.why: In Chapter 1, Who You Are, Brenen describes conviction as knowing what you believe and what you will protect even when it costs you.

options: If the team failed, the leader is powerless.
After-action questions should mostly blame the crew.
Owning the change gives you the power to change things; blame takes that away.
A good leader never reviews their own shift.
final.why: In Chapter 3, Own the Change, examining your own actions reveals a next step you can take without waiting for someone else to change.

options: Occasional intense speeches.
Changing the standard on hard days.
A leader who shows up the same way, Monday and Friday.
Setting big goals and skipping daily systems.
final.why: Chapter 6, Consistency Over Intensity, asks you to uphold a standard on ordinary days and on busy ones. That repeated action is what teammates can count on.

final.prompt: “The real job of a leader is to make other people successful” is the core of:
options: Chapter 2.
Chapter 4.
Chapter 7.
Chapter 16.
final.why: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 7: Your Job is Their Success. One way to practice it is to teach a skill and let the other person try it.

final.prompt: Which resume bullet is truthful and specific?
options: “Visionary leader who transformed team culture.”
“Ran a 5-minute recap after each weekly meeting and fixed one process issue the next week.”
“Natural born leader.”
“Managed dozens of people with no issues.”
final.why: The recap line gives an action, a frequency, and an observable result. Use a line like it only if the events happened and you can explain which process changed.

walkthroughs.title: Review a missed handoff and plan the next seven days
steps: Label the boxes with the three Chapter 3 questions. Set down one event you can describe without a name.
In this fictional club example, the meeting ended without a supplies handoff. Note one helpful action and one action the facilitator missed.
Change the last minute of the next meeting: ask who will take each remaining job and read back the agreed handoff.
Mark three real opportunities. Write the cue in advance. Use held, slipped, or no opportunity when you review each day.
Look at what the slip reveals about the cue. Choose the next small repair and set a time to check it.
narration: This is a fictional club meeting you can work through with me. Fold a sheet into three columns. Put the three after-action questions from Chapter 3 across the top. Pause for a minute and pick a meeting, practice, or work block you remember. If you prefer, stay with our club example for the whole walkthrough.

In this example I’m facilitating a supply meeting. We decided what to bring to the park cleanup. I read the list aloud and someone noticed the missing trash bags. I ended the meeting as soon as the list was complete. At the next check-in, the bags were still on the list and nobody had agreed to bring them. We know what happened. We don’t know what anyone was thinking.

In box one I write that I read back the list and gave people time to catch a missing item. I want to keep that. In box two I write that I closed the meeting before I confirmed who would bring each item. I could write that people forgot. But that would leave me guessing and wouldn’t tell me what to change. Pause for two minutes. Put a concrete action of your own in each of the first two boxes.

Here’s my third answer. At the next meeting I’ll reserve the last minute for the handoff. I’ll ask who can take each open job and read our agreements back. If no one takes a job, I’ll mark it open and ask the advisor what we can do. I can do that even if the team changes its mind about which supplies it needs. Take another minute to choose your own repair. Say it once out loud. Could someone watching tell whether you did it?

Now draw seven boxes for the week ahead. In this example I can rehearse the handoff after Monday’s project huddle, Wednesday’s volunteer planning session, and Friday’s club meeting. Beside each one I write my cue: when I reach the last agenda item, I leave one minute for the handoff. Pause for two minutes to choose three real opportunities of your own. Your days can be different.

Imagine Monday goes well. I mark held. Wednesday runs late, I shut my notebook, and I forget to check. I mark slipped. I don’t fix Wednesday by making a bigger promise. I move the reminder from the bottom of the agenda to the last item’s heading, where I will actually see it on Friday. A day with no meeting gets no opportunity. That is different from a missed promise.

Look at the three boxes and the grid together. Keep one thing that helped, own one missed action, and put the next cue where you will see it. On your third practice day, spend five minutes checking what changed and what you want to try next.

fields.label: My two or three non-negotiable standards
fields.hint: Write an action for each one and what keeping it might cost. Keep personal beliefs private.

fields.label: My ownership rewrite
fields.hint: First blame sentence → my part → one repair I can make and when.

fields.label: My after-action review
fields.hint: What went well? What did not go well? And what will I do differently tomorrow? Answer about your own choices.

fields.label: My practice plan
fields.hint: Choose one standard, a cue to take ownership and three days for a short after-action. Mark the seven-day grid below.

fields.label: One way I will help someone get better
fields.hint: What I’ll show, when they’ll practice, and how we’ll check it together.

fields.label: Optional · A trusted person I can talk to
fields.hint: A role, such as coach or advisor, is enough. You can leave this blank.
